title: PROGRESS for Indian Tribes Act
official_summary:
Practical Reforms and Other Goals To Reinforce the Effectiveness of Self-Governance and Self-Determination for Indian Tribes Act of 2019 or the PROGRESS for Indian Tribes Act

This bill replaces the Tribal Self-Governance Demonstration Project with the Tribal Self-Governance Program. Under the program, Native American tribes or organizations may receive grants to plan for participation in self-governance and to negotiate the terms of participation.

In addition, the bill revises the Department of the Interior's process for approving self-governance compacts and funding agreements with tribes. Interior must negotiate contracts and funding agreements to maximize implementation of the self-governance policy. The bill sets forth requirements for tribes participating in self-governance with respect to conflicts of interest, audits, redesign and consolidation of programs, retrocession of programs, non-duplication of funding, and records.

Funding agreements must include provisions for Interior to monitor the performance of trust functions by the tribe and to reassume a program and funding under specified circumstances.

Tribes participating in self-governance may elect to assume some federal responsibilities with respect to certain construction projects.

The bill prohibits obligating a tribe to continue performance of a compact or funding agreement that provides insufficient funding.

summary.headline: A 2020 law that reshapes how federal agencies, mainly the Interior Department, work with tribes that run their own federal programs under self-governance agreements.
summary.what_it_does: The law replaces the old Tribal Self-Governance Demonstration Project with a permanent Tribal Self-Governance Program. Tribes can get grants to plan for joining the program and to negotiate its terms. The Interior Department must follow new steps when approving the agreements, called compacts and funding agreements, that tribes use to take over federal programs. The law also sets rules for tribes in the program on conflicts of interest, audits, program changes, returning programs to the government, duplicate funding, and records. Interior keeps a role in monitoring trust functions and can take a program back in certain situations. A tribe cannot be forced to keep running a program if the funding is not enough.

who_it_affects.group: Federally recognized American Indian and Alaska Native tribes
who_it_affects.how: Tribes can apply for planning and negotiation grants and can take on more federal programs under the updated self-governance rules.
Tribal organizations can receive the same planning grants and take part in self-governance under the new program.
Interior must follow revised steps to approve compacts and funding agreements and must monitor tribal trust functions and certain construction work.

who_it_affects.group: Tribal members who receive services from programs run under self-governance
who_it_affects.how: Services are delivered by tribal governments under agreements that now include new audit, records, and performance rules.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: The law took effect when it was signed on October 21, 2020, though some specific requirements may phase in over time.
